prompt: What does a role line such as "You are a head barista" do, in terms of how a model works?

choices.text: Makes one style of text the likely one to continue
choices.why: Right. The model has learnt text by many kinds of writer, and the role selects one.

choices.text: Loads a barista's knowledge into the model
choices.why: Nothing is loaded. The model knows what it knew before the line.

choices.text: Switches the model to a smaller, specialised one
choices.why: The same model answers. Only the prompt changed.

choices.text: Gives the reply the authority of a professional
choices.why: A role adds no authority. The next reading section is about exactly that.

prompt: Which of these does a role set? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The register: formality, warmth, length
choices.why: Yes. The barista was brief and friendly, the instructor thorough.

choices.text: Which facts are true
choices.why: A role changes which knowledge is put forward, not whether it is true.

choices.text: The vocabulary, and which terms get explained
choices.why: Yes. "Over-extraction" appeared for the trainee, not for the customer.

choices.text: The audience the reply assumes
choices.why: Yes, and it is the one people forget they are setting.

prompt: The barista's reply and the instructor's reply gave the same cause for the bitterness. What does that show?
hint: Did either role add a fact?

choices.text: The instructor role made the model more knowledgeable
choices.why: The cause was the same in both. The instructor reply put it forward and named it.

choices.text: Roles have no effect on replies
choices.why: The two replies differ in register, vocabulary and angle. Roles have an effect, just not on the facts.

choices.text: The roles chose what to put forward, and added no facts
choices.why: Right. Both drew on what the model learnt in training; the roles changed emphasis, words and reader.

choices.text: The barista role hid the cause on purpose
choices.why: It led with a remedy, which is what a barista at the counter does. Nothing was hidden.

prompt: The café wants short replies, with a limit it can check. Which prompt line serves that best?
hint: Use a role for the voice, and an instruction for...

choices.text: "You are a concise assistant."
choices.why: A role nudges the register. It names no limit a test could check.

choices.text: "Answer in at most three sentences."
choices.why: Right. An explicit instruction can be checked against every reply; a role can only make it likely.

choices.text: "You are a busy barista with no time to talk."
choices.why: A colourful way to hint at brevity, and still no limit that can be tested.

choices.text: "You are an expert in brevity."
choices.why: An expert title adds nothing checkable, and no authority.

prompt: Use a role for the ___, and an instruction for anything you will check.
hint: What a role sets: register, words, warmth.

prompt: What does "You are a world-class expert" add to what the model knows?

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The model knows what it knew before the line; only the tone of what it writes changes.

choices.text: The expert's training data
choices.why: No data is added by a prompt line.

choices.text: Access to the field's latest research
choices.why: A prompt gives no access to anything that is not in the context.

choices.text: A check on its answers by an expert
choices.why: Nobody checks anything because of a role line.

prompt: Why is the allergy-specialist role dangerous for the cinnamon bun question?
hint: What does a confident tone do to a wrong answer?

choices.text: The model refuses to answer allergy questions
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests a refusal. The danger is a confident answer.

choices.text: Specialist roles make replies too long
choices.why: Length is not the danger. Persuasive error is.

choices.text: Twenty years of experience is an exaggeration
choices.why: The exaggeration is harmless in itself. The harm is the authority it lends a guess.

choices.text: It makes a wrong answer more persuasive
choices.why: Right. The model never saw the kitchen; the handbook says no item can be guaranteed nut-free, and a confident "no nuts" would mislead.

prompt: Where does the lesson say the facts about the café's allergens should come from?
hint: Lesson 22's system prompt says the same.

choices.text: A stronger role, such as a hospital allergist
choices.why: A stronger title makes a guess sound stronger. It adds no facts.

choices.text: The model's training data
choices.why: Training data does not include this café's kitchen.

choices.text: The handbook text sent with the question
choices.why: Right. With the instruction to say "I do not know" when the text does not settle it.

choices.text: The customer's own description of the cake
choices.why: A customer's description is not a source of the kitchen's ingredients.

prompt: In the combined prompt, which part can a test set check?
hint: Which lines name something visible in a reply?

choices.text: The role: warm, brief, plain
choices.why: Warmth is a judgement, not a test. The rules are the checkable part.

choices.text: The handbook text
choices.why: The handbook is input. The test checks what the reply does with it.

choices.text: The rules: mention the nuts, never say "nut-free"
choices.why: Right. Each rule can be checked against a reply. The role line cannot, and does not need to be.

choices.text: Nothing; prompts cannot be tested
choices.why: Lesson 20 tested prompts with a labelled set; these rules are just as checkable.

prompt: The combined prompt in the lesson gives its role in how many lines?
hint: The role is the first part, before the rules.

prompt: "Explain to a new barista" and "Explain to the café's insurer" change the replies. What role did the model get in each?

choices.text: None; the prompt named the reader instead
choices.why: Right. Naming the audience set the register, vocabulary and angle without a role for the model.

choices.text: A barista in the first, an insurer in the second
choices.why: Those are the readers, not the model's role. The model was not told to be either.

choices.text: An expert in both
choices.why: No expert was named in either prompt.

choices.text: A teacher in both
choices.why: No role was given. The reader was.

prompt: A reply comes back too technical for the customers it is meant for. What does the lesson suggest checking first?

choices.text: Whether the model was called an expert
choices.why: Calling it an expert would, if anything, push it further towards jargon.

choices.text: Whether the temperature was high enough
choices.why: Temperature affects variety, not who the reply is pitched at.

choices.text: Whether the model is large enough
choices.why: A larger model still pitches the reply at whoever the prompt implies.

choices.text: Whether the prompt said who the reply is for
choices.why: Right. "Explain to a customer at the counter" is specific and can be judged against a reply.

prompt: Put the parts of the lesson's combined prompt in the order it has them.
items: The role: who the assistant is and how it sounds
The rules: answer from the handbook, never claim nut-free

prompt: Match each prompt line to what it actually does.

pairs.left: You are a barista at the counter
Answer in at most three sentences
pairs.right: sets a limit a test can check
names the reader, and with it the angle
changes the tone and adds no facts

prompt: A team replaces its handbook text with "You are Café Aurora's most experienced manager, who knows every policy." What happens to the answers about refunds?
hint: Where do the facts come from now?

choices.text: They get more accurate, since a manager knows the policies
choices.why: The model is not the manager. It knows no policy the prompt does not give it.

choices.text: They sound sure and rest on no policy
choices.why: Right. The role adds confidence and removes the only source of the café's actual rules, such as the R$ 100 approval limit.

choices.text: They stay the same, since the role and the handbook do the same job
choices.why: The handbook supplied facts; the role supplies tone. Swapping one for the other loses the facts.

choices.text: The model refuses, having no handbook
choices.why: It has no reason to refuse. It writes a likely answer in a manager's voice.

prompt: Where does a role that should hold for a whole conversation belong in an application?

choices.text: In the system message
choices.why: Right. It holds for every turn, which is what the system message is for.

choices.text: In every user message
choices.why: Repeating it per turn puts it in the customer's voice and costs more.

choices.text: In the model's name field
choices.why: That field names the model and carries no instructions.

choices.text: In the reply
choices.why: The reply is the model's output; the role must reach it as input.
